In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
antifolates are transported via the RFC and the MFR, with the former transporter being of greater importance.
dietary folate deficiency may be used to improve antitumor effects for antifolates that are transported via the RFC and/or MFR.
antifolates that are polyglutamatable and that have a high affinity for RFC are most potent inhibitors of TS and are most active in vivo against L1210-RPC bearing mice on a folate-deficiency diet.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the antifolate transport dynamics of RFC/MRF may provide a basis within a new therapeutic approach to cancer chemotherapy.
the therapeutic efficacy of antifolateresistant cancer cells may be significantly improved by the combination of dietary folate depletion and antifolate treatment.
the antitumor effects observed for antifolates that are substrates for both the RFC and the MFR are dependent on the dietary folate status.
The main takeaway from our work is that

dietary folate depletion is likely to be of clinical benefit for patients with cancer that are treated with antifolates that have a high affinity for the membrane folate transporters, and are polyglutamatable.

the dynamics of membrane folate transport can be used as a basis to assess the in situ potency of TS inhibition by antifolates in vitro, and to assess the in vivo therapeutic effects of antifolares in vivo.
dietary folate status is a key determinant for the therapeutic effect of folate-based antifolates, and that this may be exploited in order to further improve their clinical activity.
